To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Active Inference theory of perception and action can accommodate the classical associative processes of animal behaviour, and in turn can explain how the brain uses interoceptive inference to regulate homeostasis.

the generative models used in Active Inference can be used to contextualise the Pavlovian, habitual and goal-directed processes that mediate associative learning, and that these processes can be understood as hierarchical contextualisations of homeostatic and interoceptive inferences.
the Active Inference theory of perception and action can account for the multiple control processes that underpin animal behaviour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what it means to be a living organism.
the question of how organisms regulate themselves in a complex environment, and how this is related to the question of how they learn.
the integration of multiple scales of inference and action, and the role of homeostatic processes in adaptive control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Active Inference is a general framework for homeostatic regulation, associative learning and adaptive behavioural control.

Active Inference is a theory that explains the emergence of adaptive behaviour, including classical associative learning processes, as a consequence of the interplay between homeostatic regulation, perception, and action.

Active Inference is a general framework for understanding how animals learn to control their own behaviour in order to maintain a healthy and stable state of the body, and how the brain can be viewed as a predictive controller that uses the body as an instrument for achieving its goals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Active Inference can be understood as a theory of associative learning and homeostatic control, and vice versa.
the brain can be understood as an embodied inference engine that is driven by homeostatic regulation.

we provide a formal framework that unifies associative learning and homeostatic control theories of adaptive behaviour, and that it provides a principled account for how priors can act as goals and drives to enslave behaviour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Active Inference formalism can be used to unify and generalize classical theories of homeostatic control and associative learning.
the Active Inference formalism can be used to describe a wide range of adaptive behaviours and that it can provide a unifying framework for associative learning theories.
the Bayesian formulation of perception and behaviour can accommodate the full spectrum of associative processes that have been identified in classical behavioural theories.
